subject: remote workers
one_liner: Publishing infrastructure for the distributed workforce. Your standup ships with a byline, an assigned editor, and an eleven-minute read time.
brand_voice_notes: Faux-corporate publishing gravitas. Byline sincerely believes that a daily status update is a piece of writing, that a piece of writing requires an editorial process, and that an editorial process requires a masthead. Every sentence is written by someone who has never once considered that this is funny. Kill fees, slots, above-the-fold, mean time to publication. The company treats a two-day review cycle as rigor rather than latency, and prices it like infrastructure. No winking, no exclamation points, no scare quotes.

hero.sub: Byline is the publishing layer for distributed teams. Pitch your Tuesday, get assigned a slot, file nineteen hundred words on why the migration slipped. Your team gets three free reads a month. Everything after that is a subscription decision.

features.title: The Editorial Desk
features.blurb: Every update is assigned to a working editor before your team is allowed to see it. Median time from filing to publication is two business days, which internal research confirms is roughly when the blocker resolves itself. The piece runs anyway.

features.title: Members-Only Blockers
features.blurb: Put the part where you say what is wrong behind the paywall. Teammates get three free reads per calendar month. After that they subscribe, or they escalate, or they guess. All three outcomes count as engagement.

features.title: Read Time as a Unit of Work
features.blurb: Timesheets are denominated in estimated minutes to read. A four-minute Thursday is a four-minute Thursday and reconciles cleanly against the sprint. Finance has stopped asking follow-up questions, which we log as adoption.

demo_screen_concept: The Byline reader, showing one published standup titled 'Q3 Migration: A Personal Accounting' inside a team publication called Field Notes. Article chrome across the top: author byline with an oil-portrait author photo, publication name, an eleven-minute read time, a filed date and a published date sitting three days apart. A left rail of clap controls with a live count that increments on click and a hard stop at your remaining quarterly allocation. Body text is selectable: highlighting a passage raises a marginal-note toolbar and reveals pinned annotations from named coworkers in the vellum margin. A members-only gate slides up over the Blockers section carrying a '2 of 3 free reads left this month' meter, dismissible only by clicking 'I am on the team'. Three tabs switch the main column between the published piece, the editor's markup with strikethroughs and queries, and the response thread. A right rail lists three sibling standups under 'More from Field Notes' with their own read times.

design_direction.style: Illuminated manuscript scriptorium, vellum daylight mode. The page is staged as a bound codex produced by a publishing company that has decided a daily status update is a text worthy of rubrication. A single warm vellum ground (#F2E8D5) runs the entire page with no dark mode, no glass, no backdrop blur, no clay volume, no bento lattice, no blister-pack die lines, no drafting hairlines and no trophy shelving. Depth comes only from ruling: every surface is the same flat vellum, separated by 1px oak-gall rules and a repeating horizontal scribe-line grid (a repeating-linear-gradient at 2rem pitch, 6% opacity) that runs under body copy like the pricked and ruled lines of a manuscript page. The organising move is the two-column codex block: a wide text measure of 62 to 68 characters set flush left with a narrow marginal gutter to its left, and every section header rubricated in vermilion (#8E1B12) small caps with generous letterspacing. The core motif is the versal: a large drop-cap initial in a gold-leaf ochre square (#9A7A1E at low opacity fill, 2px vermilion border, near-square 2px radius) floated into the first two lines of each major block, built in pure CSS with float and initial-letter fallbacks, never an image. Marginalia are the secondary motif: small vermilion pilcrows, hairline-boxed annotations set in the outer margin at 0.78rem, and a running head above each section in letterspaced small caps. Pricing tiers are laid out as three ruled columns of an ordinance table under a single continuous gold rule, not as floating cards with shadows. Nothing casts a shadow anywhere on the page. Nothing has a border radius above 3px. Rules do all structural work.

fonts.display: 'Cormorant Garamond', 'EB Garamond', Garamond, 'Times New Roman', serif

design_direction.archetype: Long-form publishing platform product page issued as a bound codex: rubricated hero colophon, ruled feature quires, an ordinance table for pricing, and portrait testimonials set as commendations.
design_direction.motion_vocab: Ink-settling restraint. Nothing slides, bounces or springs. Rules draw themselves in on scroll via a scaleX transform from the left over 420ms ease-out, staggered 60ms per section. Versal initials fade from 0 to 1 opacity over 300ms. Hover states change ink colour and underline thickness only, 160ms, never position. Clap and tab interactions in the demo cross-fade at 140ms. Every transition is disabled under prefers-reduced-motion.
design_direction.hero_composition_notes: No hero image. The hero is a colophon block: a letterspaced vermilion running head reading the publication name, then the h1 set in Cormorant Garamond at clamp(2.6rem, 7vw, 5.6rem) with a tight 0.98 line-height and an oversized gold versal on the first word, then the sub paragraph held to a 60-character measure in the left two thirds. A single gold rule closes the block full-bleed. Below the rule, a three-cell ruled colophon strip carries the stats in small caps: median time to publication, free reads per month, and claps per manager per quarter. The primary CTA sits inline under the sub as a solid vermilion block with square corners, not a pill.

images.rationale: Landing hero skipped: the direction is a rubricated typographic colophon with a CSS gold versal, and a photograph in that slot would fight the codex conceit. Demo hero also skipped for the same reason, and the reader's article art is handled as an illuminated CSS panel. Budget went to portraits, where the manuscript style has a genuine precedent: three testimonial commendation portraits on the landing page plus one byline author portrait for the demo reader. All four are muted oil-on-panel paintings on a vellum ground so they read as plates bound into the codex rather than stock headshots.
